slides.headline: This salamander never grows up.
slides.sub: And that is exactly why scientists can't stop studying it

slides.headline: It keeps its gills for life
slides.body: Most salamanders lose their gills and move onto land. The axolotl stays aquatic and keeps its feathery external gills as an adult. The trait is called neoteny.

slides.headline: Lose a leg? It grows a new one.
slides.body: Axolotls regenerate entire limbs and tails over a few months, and can repair parts of the heart, spinal cord and brain without scarring.

slides.label: base pairs in its genome, about 10× a human's
slides.body: Yet it has a similar number of protein-coding genes to us. The extra DNA is mostly repeated sequences.

slides.headline: The wild ones live in one place
slides.body: Only the canals and wetlands of Xochimilco, on the edge of Mexico City. Pet axolotls are a separate captive-bred lineage, often leucistic (pale) like the one on slide 1.

slides.headline: Critically Endangered
slides.body: Surveys found about 6,000 per km² in 1998 and roughly 100 per km² by 2008. The 2020 IUCN assessment estimates just 50–1,000 adults remain in the wild.

caption:
The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) never grows up, and it can regrow its own limbs, spinal cord and parts of its brain.

It keeps its larval gills for life, carries a genome ten times the size of ours, and in the wild survives in exactly one place: the canals of Xochimilco, Mexico City, where it is Critically Endangered.
